[Nurse A ], we concluded on Friday -- good morning, I should say -- with the events on 8 June 2015 and concerning [Baby A]. I would like to move on now, please, to events the following night, 9 June.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you were on duty that night?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I was.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your shift was 7.30, commencing at 7.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you told us on Friday about the routine of the initial huddle and then going to the bedside for your, as it were, bespoke handover for the baby for whom you were designated. If I could just ask Mr Murphy, please, to go initially to slide 143 on [Baby B]'s sequence of events, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think we need to click into it. We can see there your arrival at 7.27 that evening via the swipe system on the door to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we move on, please, to slide 145. If we can go into that slide, please. We can see there represented on the table those who were on duty, including the consultants, the registrar and senior house officer, nurses and nursery nurses.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Next slide, please, Mr Murphy. This is a diagram of the location of various babies, the staff that were allocated in the context of the neonatal unit itself.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you see that clearly, [Nurse A ]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see, in nursery 1, [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You, according to this, can you confirm, were the designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I was.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And according to you, you had a second, certainly for part of the shift, a second designated baby in the same nursery, JE?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I hadn't remembered that. If that's the case --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. We can see from this that, in nursery 3, Lucy Letby had two babies allocated, located in nursery 3?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I won't take you through all of them. Do you recall who you took over from on the day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I think it was Jo Williams.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Were any concerns raised with you about [Baby B]'s welfare during the course of the day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. She'd had a good day from what I recall. The parents had been there and had cuddles and [Baby B] had had a good day.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just a little bit of trouble hearing you from behind me. I'm so sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I didn't remind you this morning, my fault. Just try and keep that voice up so the back row of the jury -- then we can be confident --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Sorry. I don't remember any concerns being handed over to me. [Baby B] had had a good day, had continued to improve from my memory. Obviously mum and dad were very upset, I know they had cuddles, so it was -- just handover was unremarkable and that she, thankfully, was doing well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You mentioned mum and dad.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you see them during the course of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. Mum and dad, I think, were there during handover and for the first part of my shift. Mum was still fairly recently after her caesarean, they were still -- mum was still, I believe, an inpatient upstairs and I know that dad and grandma had permission to stay as well, from what I recall.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Did there come a point where they left?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, there did. I'd gone over the plan with them for [Baby B]'s care for the night. They wanted to know if anything changed at all, no matter how small. I'd reassured them that obviously if anything changed I would make sure that if I couldn't come and tell them, somebody else would contact them. I reassured them the best I could that we were happy with how [Baby B] was progressing, that we had no concerns about how she was at that point. She was doing well and I encouraged them to go and try and get some rest, but also that they could come, all of them or one of them, at any point in the night or phone down at any point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Did there come a point where they did accept your encouragement and go and get some rest?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I think they knew they had to look after themselves as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So returning to your duties, I think you -- certainly we've heard that there are checks that are undertaken when you first come on duty --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- to satisfy yourself everything is shipshape and Bristol fashion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you, thereafter, maintain hourly observations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, because [Baby B] was receiving CPAP, then she would have hourly observations and less regular temperature checks. We do those hourly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I'm not going to take you to them on the sequence of events, but were those checks carried out each hour through the night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, we document them every hour. You're in the room, you are constantly looking and aware if the monitors alarm at all, and then we document them every hour and document how much has gone through on the infusions and things.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember leaving nursery 1 during the early part of your shift up until about midnight that night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I can't confirm at all whether I left. It wouldn't have been for long if I did, maybe to get something or...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just dealing then with that period, could I ask Mr Murphy, please, to take us to 150.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can click into that, please. This is a note you wrote retrospectively at about -- well, at 5.45 the following morning --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- but it covers the period I have just asked you about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the analyst's summary of what you write. We can go and check it in a moment. But between 8 pm and 00.20, if I can put it that way:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Continued on CPAP in air for start of shift."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were telling us before she was on CPAP, which we know is breathing assistance, but just with air:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Tolerated well, no bradys."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That I think is a --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Bradycardia, slow heart rate.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. And desats which is, I think, a fall in oxygen level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: In oxygen level.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Tolerating 3ml DEBM..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Donor-expressed breast milk.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... two-hourly."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "All obs satisfactory. Active and handling well."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could I just ask Mr Murphy to go to the original note, please, to ensure that that's all we need.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it's on the right-hand side about halfway down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)

While there's a hold-up, I can -- I don't know whether others can make it out on the screen. It's about halfway down on the right-hand side and I think, I hope I can say this, it's exactly what it says on the tin. It's what the analyst has put on the page before.
So if we can perhaps move on from there while the computer catches up.

I want to ask you, please, and I've mentioned that your hourly reviews appear on this sequence of events, but I'm going to move ahead, please, to a note that you made about an incident just before midnight on 9 June.
It's at entry 210, please.
We'll rely on the summary for now and then we'll double-check it:
"Shortly before midnight [Baby B] desaturated to 75%."
NURSE A: Yes.
Perhaps if you just refresh your memory from that and tell us what you recall of that incident.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So CPAP is given just nasally on babies, either by prongs or a mask.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pausing there, prongs -- two, as it were, tubes that go inside the nose?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. They're very short and quite wide, so they fill the nostrils, so you get a good seal. And the mask sits round the nose so you get a good seal and they're held on, secured to a hat, a special hat.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The masks or the prongs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Both.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are the prongs part of the mask?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, they're separate. You can change that little bit of the interface from one to the other if need be. So [Baby B] had prongs in at this point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You say that they're secured by the hat?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just tell us how that works.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: The hats are fitted, so you have to measure the baby's head and get the right size hat. And then the interface of the CPAP has two little ties from it that then weave through three holes on each side of the hat so they hold it securely in place.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For those who can't see, you're indicating this sort of area here (indicating) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, there's holes up the side of the hat --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and that's where they pass through?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- and they take those through the three holes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The tape I should say, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How were you alerted to the fact the prongs had --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So the CPAP driver, the machine, will have sounded an alarm to say the pressure's dropped and also [Baby B]'s monitor alarmed to say her oxygen level had dropped. So though I said in the other note she'd had no bradycardias or desaturations and her levels dropped here, it was because she had knocked or moved
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: and her prongs had come out. So I would have classed a desaturation as something that happened when nothing else had changed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. I'm guessing not, from what you told us, but is that an unusual thing to happen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. I mean, you secure the CPAP securely but you can't do it too tightly because that's going to be really uncomfortable for the babies and cause indents and even their skin to break down. So it's got to be as secure as you can get it to get the seal, but if the baby moves then it can come out and sometimes, as babies start to feel better, they push it out themselves sometimes because it's there on their face.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You note here suggests:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Took a little while to recover."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, and I gave her a little bit of oxygen but that's not uncommon. CPAP provides a pressure that, though [Baby B] was doing all her breathing herself, it takes a little bit of the work out of it because it helps keep the lungs a little bit inflated --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- when she breathes out. So there's a chance that maybe her air sacs in her lungs had closed down a little bit and it just took a little while for the CPAP to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your note continues:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "HR remained stable."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Heart rate.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good resp effort throughout."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So breathing well, not -- you know, making a good breathing effort.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once settled CBG taken?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Capillary blood gas.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which was normal, according to the note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And as it happened, this suggests Dr Lambie was on the unit. Do you remember speaking to Dr Lambie?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Not directly, but I must have done. I'd have probably just said, "Oh, [Baby B]'s prongs came out". I can't remember whether she was actually -- she may well have been due a blood gas around that time anyway or I may have decided to do it because she had the desaturation after her prongs had come out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You mentioned that [Baby B] was receiving some milk.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was she being fed in any other way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: She had an infusion going through her -- I think she had a long line at that point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Infusion? Could you explain that to us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So what you might call a drip, an intravenous bag of fluids with a line going through a pump at a set rate through -- I think she had a long line at that point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Perhaps if we could go to 212, please. Is there a particular name for the fluids that you were talking about being on the drip?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I was going to say TPN, but it's the Babiven.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Total parenteral nutrition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the full title and is Babiven the brand name, is it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Presumably you call it both during the course --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: And the lipids is part of that as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about that in a second. I suspect you've settled on what's almost in the centre of the page where it says "Babiven start-up"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And to the left it says "LL", does that assist with how she was receiving it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, long line, as I thought.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in addition to the milk, she was on a drip of nutrition, fluid nutrition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was travelling via the long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about the long line from Dr Harkness, but that was via a long line. I think you mentioned it went via a pump.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. So to make sure that the right amount is given, the line coming -- the infusion line coming from the bag of fluid goes through a special pump where it can monitor -- well, it delivers a set rate, whatever you set the rate on the pump to. It also detects if there's an air bubble coming down from the bag. It can detect the pressure going -- that's it taking to put the fluid through the line. What else? You can set it to infuse a set amount, so it'll stop infusing once -- it depends what you are using it for.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it effectively regulates --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- what's going in --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and, as you said, will detect an air bubble that comes down the line from the TPN?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would it allow it to pass through?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. So especially with TPN, because that's under a cover, a plastic bag that you can't see through because it has to be protected from the light, if the bag empties and air starts coming down then that'll detect it and stop the infusion so it doesn't go any further.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. For those of us who have never been in a ward with this sort of thing, where does the bag sit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So on -- it's on a drip stand, so it's hanging on the drip stand and then --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It has to be above the patient, does it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It has to be above the machine really -- so that's if it's a bag. For Babiven it would be a bag.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right and it has a set rate that you put in the pump?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have to cover the bag, did you say, because it's affected by light --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Light sensitive, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And how long ordinarily would a bag be expected to last?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: For most of our babies the bags lasted for the full 48 hours because they were having such a small amount per hour. And then they got changed 48-hourly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We may go into this in a bit more detail in later cases, but it's described as "start-up Babiven" on this feeding chart or this intensive care chart. Is it always start-up or does that change?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, so we had start-up bags that were stocked on the unit --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does the name pretty well tell us what they're there for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. It has a slightly different... Slightly... Um...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because it's got various trace elements and things in it. So it has slightly different combination of things than later bags.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that designed for a particular stage of a baby's life?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: When it starts, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And what succeeds the start-up formula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: At Chester it was often made up -- it was -- there were sort of follow-on standard bags that followed on, but most of
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: the time, based on blood results, the doctor would order specific bags for --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And do you know where they would be made up?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: In CIVAS, which is the sterile drugs preparation department.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not in the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. If we could then move please to the next slide, 213. This document is headed:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Prescription confirmation for neonatal parenteral nutrition."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we can see on the top left underneath that particular heading, "[Baby B]".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby B] allocated her mum's surname at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down we can see various measurements of Peditrace, Solivito and water?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And on the right, the elemental content?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's mention underneath on the left:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Lipid feed supplied in separate syringe."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you mentioned that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just hold on a second because I'd like to scroll down the document a little bit more, please. More again, please, Mr Murphy. Some handwriting towards the bottom.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we pause there. At the top:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "For administration for up to 48 hours commencing at a time before midnight on 9 June."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see a signature from the pharmacist?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then handwritten, "Lipid", a reference number?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A date?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we've just gone past midnight by the look of it because the time to the right is 00.05.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that to denote the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So five past midnight. Do you recognise the signature underneath?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I do.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Whose is that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Lucy Letby's.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How does lipid or how is lipid administered to the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It comes in a syringe, which you connect to an infusion line. And rather than going through a pump, the syringe goes into what we call a syringe driver. Again, that can be programmed to -- that's programmed for a set rate and/or a set volume, depending what you need.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So does that not enter then the same long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Further down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Further down?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. So they're connected further down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So there's a connection on the long line to allow other things to be added through it; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. Some long lines are double lumen, which means they've got two separate sides running down the one line. I honestly don't know whether [Baby B] had a single lumen or a double lumen. With IV you can then put a sort of connector on that means you can run two or more things together, so they join just before they go into the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Do they join before the pump or after the pump?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: After the pump.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we could scroll down, I think there's a second page on this, please. If we go -- so this is another record of the administration of the fluid, the neonatal parenteral nutrition we've been taking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down, we see [Baby B]'s name on the top right, and if we scroll down to day 3 in the left-hand box, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So day 3 of [Baby B]'s life?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 9 June. If we read across, please, the top line: Babiven Maintenance, Solivito and Peditrace. We can see some measurements there. If we go across, we see what appears to be "A Brunton".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Who --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Dr Brunton.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you, yes, we've heard already from Dr Brunton.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we continue to read across, tell me please what the date and time signify, 10 June at 00.05.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So it's the time it was put up and started, the bag was changed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. In the left hand -- to the left hand of that, are they two signatures?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Whose are they, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: The top one is mine, the [Initials of Nurse A]. And underneath is Lucy's, Lucy Letby's.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Is there a reason why there are two signatures?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Because everything has to be double-checked.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in the case of TPN, briefly what does doublechecking involve?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Making sure that it's prescribed correctly, checking the bags and date, that the bag is for who it says it is, if it's a specific bag. We used to check that what was written on the sheet that you showed before, the list of things, matched the list of things that was on the label on the bag.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Putting it up and checking that the rate and the pump is correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Is that a strict rule for two people?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is there any significance in one signature appears to be over the other, is there any significance in that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Not necessarily. I think on some charts, not on this, where the diagonal line divides the box, it may say first checker, you know, administrator and checker. But quite often whoever signs it first will sign in one place and whoever signs it second will sign in the other.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And if we go to the row below, there's the lipid being introduced, is it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we have the same -- if we go over to the right-hand side, we can see in fact two times, there's 10 June at 00.05?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And there's also 23.55. Can you help with us that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't know what that top column is. That far right, if we -- I can't remember what... Oh, "date and time finished". So that's the time and date, so I've put it up at 00.05 and then, on the following shift, I've changed it to 23.55.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's what that means. Just the lipid --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So we do it 24-hourly so --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's next to the lipid? Is that just the lipid that would have been changed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, because the bags lasted 48 hours.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As well as the TPN?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, the TPN, the Babiven that we put up on the 10th at 00.05 would have lasted 48 hours from then.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just scrolling to the top document again, and particularly the signature, is there any reason why this has been signed again, do you know?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So it's signing to say that we've double-checked it with the bag. You can see the lipid and the number underneath it is the number off the syringe, so just to record the batch number of the syringe.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your signature not there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, my signature is not there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does that tell you anything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Quite possibly an oversight because I've signed it on the other two charts.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. So lipids and TPN hung, if I can use your term, at 00.05?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go on to the next slide, please, 214.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Go into the document, thanks. Go to the foot of the document.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: An observation chart. We've seen these before. If we can scroll down. This is -- I'm sorry, can we check the times on the top of this, please? I should have done that first. The document itself, just the times across the top of it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: This is the fourth column.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This starts at 9 pm as opposed to midnight. It starts at 9 pm. The date on the top is 10 June.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But most of the form, of course, will be 10 June, so I don't know whether we can read anything into that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could we scroll down to the bottom, please? We talked before about your hourly checks.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Looking at the bottom, does the nurse who's done the checks initial the bottom of the form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the first three initials, do you recognise those?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: They're mine.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. There's a gap at midnight but you've told us what you were doing around midnight. Is that significant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I think... Have I recorded -- are other observations recorded higher up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we scroll up just that column, please, and doublecheck it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, the heart rate and the respirations have been done.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She didn't need her temperature doing. I haven't written in the incubator temperature and the humidity.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm guessing either something interrupted me finishing the bottom of the chart --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. We may come to that in a minute. The 1 o'clock entry, they're not your initials?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recognise whose they are?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: They're Lucy Letby's.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember why Lucy Letby might have been doing those observations at 1 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Quite likely because it was just after [Baby B] had had an episode and I would have been in the room, but maybe I was talking to parents or doing something else with [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Well, you mention an episode.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you tell us, firstly, what time you think that episode was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Um... Around half past midnight, maybe just before.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can look at the note in a minute, but I'd just like to first of all see what you remember. Tell us about what you remember, please, of that incident.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So I remember I was -- I had gloves on, I was drawing medication up -- I can't tell you which baby it was for.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As we said, there was another baby in the room.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where were you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I was standing -- so in the intensive care room, [Baby B] was at the far end and there's sort of a half wall across and I was just by there. I couldn't see [Baby B] directly but, you know, I was in the room and if I looked down the wall I could see her.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Why couldn't you see [Baby B] directly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Just because of the half wall --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Were you on the other side then of the half wall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Okay. Why would you have gloves on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Because I was drawing intravenous medication up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. All right. Sorry, I interrupted you. You're in nursery 1, you have told us where you were.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: [Baby B]'s monitor alarmed and Lucy went to her because I was in the middle of preparing the drugs. So Lucy went to her.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where had Lucy been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Standing with me checking the medication.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: And then Lucy said, "She's apnoeic, she's not breathing", and asked me to go and help.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. And did you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did anyone else go to the cot with you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: There was -- I believe there was only the two of us in the room at that point, so I went over. Sometimes babies do become apnoeic, have too long a pause in their breathing, so, you know, we're used to dealing with that and quite often they recover quickly from that. If they don't then you ask for help from doctors.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did [Baby B] recover quickly from that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what happened next?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: We had to use the Neopuff to give her breaths because she wasn't breathing herself. She was very pale, she had a blotchy -- blotchiness to her skin. Dr Lambie came and we had to resuscitate her and we called [Dr B] in -- I think she was at home at that point, but she was the consultant on call that night. However, [Baby B] did recover well and didn't need any resuscitation medication.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can I break that down a little bit? So you go over, she didn't, did you say, initially respond?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So was it you who administered the Neopuff? Is that your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: (Pause). I may have done for a short while. I'm certain that by the time [Dr B] and parents arrived, I was on the other side of the incubator.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. How did -- when you were at the incubator, how did [Baby B] appear?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: She suddenly looked very ill. She looked very like her brother had done the night before with the pale, white -- with this purple blotchy discolouration (indicating).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you were indicating your chest, I think, with your hand.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just whereabouts was it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Generally. From my recollection, it was all over. I'm doing this (indicating), but yeah, I...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you describe where on her body you saw it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It was all over from what I recollect.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You mentioned it was like her brother's?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, as I said on Friday, when we were -- that's how [Baby A] had appeared too. I just... I just remember thinking, "No, not again", you know.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: As I said on Friday, I'd not seen anything like that before and then to see his sister with the same appearance... Um...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You mentioned putting out a call, an emergency call. We've heard a little bit about that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I know Dr Lambie had been on the ward shortly before because I'd done the blood gas and discussed it with her and I can't remember whether she'd left or whether she was still on the unit at the time. I know she was there quite quickly and I know we asked for [Dr B] at the same time because we were so concerned because of what had happened with [Baby A] the night before. And I also asked for somebody to go straight upstairs and get mum and dad and --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay. What did, if anything, Dr Lambie do when she arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I know we intubated [Baby B], so put the breathing tube in.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Any other measures necessary at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: We were breathing for her. I think she had a few chest compressions as well, but then didn't need any medication. Her heartbeat was good, heart rate was back.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's then have a look, if we can, please, at the note that you made at the time. 218, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just have a quick read of that for me, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
NURSE A: Yes.
We're just going to see if we can get the original note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a note, I'm going to suggest -- do you recognise making the note that you made?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I've seen the original previously and, yes, that's how I recall the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So written in retrospect at 7.29 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Headed "Significant events":
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "00.30. Sudden desaturation to 50%. Cyanosed in appearance."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So bluish --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- tinge.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Centrally shut down"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So very pale, not a good capillary refill, so peripherally there's not much circulation going on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How do you remember measure capillary refill time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: You can -- by pressing on the chest area for 5 seconds and then releasing and counting how long it takes for the colour to return.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Limp and apnoeic"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "CMV"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Continuous mandatory ventilation, so breaths via the Neopuff mask.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. And "chest movement seen". And then:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Colour changed rapidly to purple blotchiness with white patches. Starting to become bradycardic.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Emergency call for doctors put out. Continued with Neopuff via Guedel airway."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's a Guedel airway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It's a little airway that you can put in. It sits over the tongue and holds the tongue out of the way. It's got a hole down the middle of it so you can then put the mask on. It's just a little more -- it's a way of making sure the airway's secure so you can give the breaths.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How long did this -- are you able to say -- collapse continue for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Um... My recollection is that she did start to stabilise quite quickly, maybe 10/15 minutes of -- and she was looking better.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Did the family come --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- in response to your alert?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next note that you made of what followed is at 2.30, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is a continuation by the look of it of the note you made at 7.29?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It continues on from the last:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... [until] Dr Lambie arrived. Became bradycardic to 80s. Successfully intubated [I think that should say] by Dr Lambie and HR improved quickly."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's heart rate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "0.9% saline bolus given and colour started to improve almost as quickly as it had deteriorated."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which colour was that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: The purply/white blotches.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Started to breathe for self. Morphine commenced and placed on ventilator."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you give the rate as "30 SIMV"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Just a mode of delivering ventilation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What does the 20/6 stand for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So that's the pressures. So the 20 is the peak inspiratory pressure, so that's the highest pressure they're breathing in. The 6 is the peak, the peak -- end expiratory pressure. And that's -- so that's the same as the CPAP provides. It's just keeping a little bit of pressure in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the highest and the lowest?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that's at 00.50?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you add that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Parents had been called to the unit as requested after doctors had been contacted. Kept fully informed throughout at cot side."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So how did [Baby B] fare after her recovery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: She did well. I looked after her again the following night and she was back on CPAP, she'd been extubated, taken off the ventilator, in the day, and she did well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So you had the following night shift as well?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, I believe.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Beginning 10 June?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Any other significant collapses or alarms?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I haven't taken you through them, but the jury have seen on the sequence of events quite a few messages between you and Ms Letby by WhatsApp. Was that a regular occurrence, you chatting on the WhatsApp?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: We were friends.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I'm not going to take you through them all. I'd just like to ask you about one of them, please, which is at 297.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's a message from you to Lucy Letby. From what you told us, that was the third of those night shifts with [Baby B] --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- that you described. And you tell her:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We also have a 30/40..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So pregnancy is 40 weeks' gestation, so this baby was 30 weeks' gestation --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- so 10 weeks early.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "800 grams" is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, little for 30 weeks.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. And, "New twins" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- "T1 girl, T2 boy"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Boy vented and in [Baby A]'s space."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, is that the twin boy or is that the first baby that you're talking about? Can you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The jury are going to hear about a 30-week baby weighing 800 grams and born on 10 June. Do you happen to remember the baby's name that you were talking about in that message?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Um... Only because of this.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I won't take that any further.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have no more questions for you, thank you. If you wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

[Nurse A], I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of Lucy Letby. I'm going to ask some questions that deal with some general matters first of all and then we'll have a look at some of what happened with [Baby A] and some of the things that happened with [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just by way of general matters, just some questions about the kind of babies you look after in the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can I ask you about that first?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: So at this time Chester was a level 2 unit, so it could look babies from 27 weeks' gestation and above.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They can be quite fragile little children, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: They can, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And they require careful observation whilst they're with you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And it's important, isn't it, to be able to spot problems early on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because they can deteriorate rapidly if a problem takes hold, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: They can, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In your experience -- this is general, I'm not talking about the particular cases we're talking about here -- but generally, bradycardia, which is a slowing heartbeat, is not unusual in neonates?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And desaturations, so when the breathing rate changes and the oxygen in their blood lowers, that can happen as well, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And there are occasions when they can even be apnoeic, so they stop breathing for a period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've heard something about the handling, the actual practicalities of handling these kind of little babies.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And something which can happen is the mere act of handling can make them stressed, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: It can, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And it's in fact possible for them to desaturate on handling? I'm not talking about [Baby A] or [Baby B] at this point, these are general points.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: They can, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They can desaturate on handling. If you, I'm asking about you, see one of the babies who may be has a slight desaturation
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: or some initial issue, do you always intervene or do you sometimes just wait to see what happens next?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: It could be that you wait to see. You wouldn't wait indefinitely to see.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. But might you wait just to see if, I think the expression is, self-corrects?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If a baby is on a ventilator and there's an apparent desaturation, depending on the size of the desaturation, might you wait then to see if the baby self-corrects?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Um... You might in certain circumstances.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it depends on the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So obviously if it was some enormous drop in oxygen, you'd probably react very quickly to call for help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it was at an early stage, you might just wait to see if it self-corrects?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: It'd partly depend on the baby.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then [Baby B] had been good throughout the evening for me, she'd been good throughout the day, that was my handover on her, she'd been good throughout the evening.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But again, she became ill very quickly, she deteriorated very quickly, and then this colouring -- I mean, I know now that it was not related to mum's medical condition at all, but because of the suddenness of [Baby A]'s collapse I know there had been concerns that did that play any part.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is 24 hours later. It's just a little more.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We didn't know, we didn't have any answers to what had happened with [Baby A]. And you never want any baby to die, you know. We want to help them all go home with their families. blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby A].

blocks.text: All over.

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: herself and recovered, but it took about half an hour for her colour to improve. So the patches weren't there for 30 minutes but it took that time for her general greyness to disappear and her normal pink colour to return.

blocks.text: I have then written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.speaker: LAMBIE
