I do recall I was worried that we were peri-arrest or about to arrest, the heart was about to stop, because of her discolouration and her heart rate dropping. So I've decided to intubate, which means putting a breathing tube, an ET tube, through her mouth into her lungs. Size 3 to 3.5 is quite normal for a child that age.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: The first -- I've written "second attempt" so the first one wasn't successful so I have put a second one in and it is successful. I've secured it 7 centimetres at the lips. That's normal for a child that age. The reason you document that is if you need to re-intubate her it helps the next person know where the tube can sit. And I have put in brackets:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Vocal cords look normal."
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So that means I have had a good view when I have put the tube in and there wasn't anything abnormal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have then given a bolus -- NaCl is sodium chloride or salty water. We use that as part of resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I've given her 10ml per kilo, which is a standard value volume for a child. The reason for that is to give the heart a bit more blood to push against. The heart works more effectively if you stretch the muscle, so as part of resuscitation you very often give them some salty water.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "CRF" means capillary refill time. That's when you press the chest for 3 seconds and let go and you want it to be round about 2 to 3 seconds. And what -- you're trying to look at how effectively the heart is working to do that --
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- that (overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt. When you press the skin and you release, what are you looking for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I'm looking -- it needs to flash back within about 2 to 3 seconds.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I've written 3 to 4, which fits with the situation, telling me that her heart isn't working quite as well as it should be or her body is shutting down, so it's taking that little bit longer for that blood to come to the surface.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then I've written she's responded well. So after the intervention, her capillary refill has gone back down to 2, 3 seconds, so I've explained what I've done and her capillary refill is getting better.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Within 10 minutes she's becoming active and breathing. So within 10 minutes of my breathing for her with her endotracheal tube and all the above interventions, she's now starting to wriggle and move herself and breathe for herself.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt again. What does that tell you in this context?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What I have done has worked, so the interventions I have done have worked and she is recovering.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: That activity, that movement is all a positive sign of recovery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've then written "Morphine bolus [tick]". That tells me I'm planning to keep her on the ventilator. If you have a child that's alert -- becoming alert and wriggling, they don't like being ventilated, so it's kind to give them some morphine to settle them on the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: What's the effect of the morphine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's to sedate them.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: All right. I've interrupted again, I do apologise.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not at all. I have then requested bloods to be done urgently. "Coag" is coagulation, to check the blood is able to clot itself correctly. "FBC" is full blood counts. U&Es is urea and electrolytes, that's kidney function. CRP is a protein marker that looks for inflammation. Dimer is another protein that looks for inflammation. And fibrinogen is part of the blood.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: A lot of these markers will be high or low depending on if there's infection. That's the main thing we're looking for.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you want me to continue?
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Placed on" -- so she's already on the ventilator so that means I have hooked her on to ventilator and I'm planning to keep her on it. I have written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Needing morphine infusion to settle."
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So you start with a bolus to sedate her and make her feel more calm and then you continue that with a continuous infusion. Infusion just means you're giving that morphine continuously rather than in one umph --
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I think when you said continuously you mean --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ongoing.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Ongoing but not morphine going in all the time?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, it's a controlled drip so it keeps them --
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: On a timed driver, presumably, so much in at such and such a time?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Then I've written "[Dr B] arrived". That's [Dr B] who would have been my consultant on call at that time.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: This is written chronologically. That's the stage where [Dr B] arrived. That's after we've had this movement and this activity and signs of improvement?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Judging by what I've written, yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: All right, thanks. If we can carry on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have then documented the gradual improvement in her perfusion. So perfusion is blood supply, particularly to the skin, "over the next 30 minutes" that says. I've given a second bolus of 10ml per kilo. Again, it's standard to give the fluid in packets of 10ml per kilo rather than overloading a child.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And that fluid, again, is that saline again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's salty water, saline, yes. Again that would be me wanting to make sure that her perfusion is staying well so I am not happy with her completely so I have given her a second to make sure that her heart has got enough fluid to pump against.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then what follows is ABC, so this is a way of documenting -- making sure you haven't forgotten anything. So a lot of doctors follow an ABC approach when they're looking after children and then documenting it. So A is airway. ETT is the endotracheal tube or that breathing tube that I've put in her mouth. It's a 3 tube, which is fine for her, set at 7 centimetres at the lips. T1 on the X-ray that's -- I have done an X-ray and on the X-ray you look where the tip of the tube is and that's the bone in the chest and that's where it should be sitting, so I know it's in the correct position.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Very good, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: B is breathing. SIMV is referring to the mode of ventilation we use, so it's the way the machine is delivering that oxygen.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: 20/6, that's the pressure that the machine is using and that's fairly standard for a baby that age. A rate of 30 is 30 breaths a minute, which again is normal for a child that age.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Capital A in a circle means she is in air and her saturations are 96. That means the amount of oxygen in her blood is 96% adequate.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Pausing there, the significance of her being in air?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was very important. So I wasn't needing to give any supplemental oxygen.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Is that another sign of improvement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, but it's also a sign, a very positive sign.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So if this was caused by sepsis or an infection, for example, she wouldn't necessarily be in air, I'd be expecting to need to give her supplemental oxygen. So air tells me that she's in a good state at this moment in time.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So no additional oxygen required?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Sorry, I interrupted again. We've got a diagram.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a diagram of the chest. So that's of the lungs.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: The left-hand one has a kink in it because that's where your heart would be. And the arrow going through it means that's normal. So that means I've listened with a stethoscope, I couldn't hear anything out of the ordinary, and that's my way of documenting it.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I've already written "good" -- "AE" is air entry and "BL" is bilaterally. So I've listened with a stethoscope, I can't hear anything that's worrying me.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Bilaterally means both sides?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Both sides.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "CHR" is chest X-ray. "Nil acute" means nothing acute. So at that moment in time there were no changes on that X-ray that I could see.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And again, I would be looking for: is there a collapsed lung, is there an infection, anything that could explain what had happened. And I couldn't see anything on that chest X-ray at that time.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Gas" means a blood gas. That's a specific blood test looking at all the different parts of her blood to do with air, carbon dioxide, and that's all -- it's not hugely out of ordinary considering what had just appeared.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So A is airway, B is breathing, C is cardiovascular, which is the heart and also the blood vessels and the skin. Her heart rate at this time is 130/140, which back up to the normal for a child her age.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Perfusion improving peripherally" means the blood supply to her skin on the outer bits of her body is now improving. "Centrally" means the chest particularly and that's 2 to 3 seconds, which is much more back to normal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Her blood pressure 48 -- "mean" means the average, "peripheral" means I've done it on the arm or on the leg and that's okay for her.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next -- "abdo" is abdomen. That's a standard way of depicting an abdomen in medical notes. So what you are looking at is -- the two lines at the top are where the abdomen joins the chest here (indicating) and then it goes down to the bottom of the legs. And the four lines going to the side are your sides. I have written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Abdo [abdomen] is full and mildly distended."
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: That means it's a little bit bloated to look at.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: That's not hugely unusual because we've just been pumping air and oxygen into her body. Quite often you get a little bit that gets trapped in the stomach. So the fact that I have written mildly distended is not a big surprise.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "No bleeding from the umbilicus."
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have written that because sometimes if you have a collapse because of sepsis or a severe infection it can affect the bleeding, how easily your blood clots, and you can oozing of blood from the umbilicus. I don't know if that refers back to something that happened in the previous few days, I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Bowel sounds are normal."
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Again, if you have a tummy that is big and bloated you worry that that could be a sign of infection, in which case -- in the tummy, in which case the bowel sounds are very quiet or not there at all, but I have documented they were there and they are healthy.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you. I think the next -- is that AFN?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, AFN is your anterior fontanelle, so the soft spot on a baby, and N in a circle is normal. Again, if you have a baby who's very unwell with an infection or meningitis, anything like that, you can get increased pressure in the brain and the soft spot will literally bulge, so I have written that it is normal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have written that she is moving all four limbs, so that's your arms and your legs, she's moving them. The tick is she's moving them okay.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have written -- "imp" is my impression. So this is a very unusual event that I hadn't seen before or after. And I've written:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Could this be widespread sepsis?"
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So sepsis is a severe infection that's spreading through the bloodstream:
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Could this be a coagulopathy?"
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Coagulation is how easily your blood clots and "opathy" means there is a problem with it. So I'm asking myself: is there a problem with her blood clotting? Then I've grouped them both together, "DIC".
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: DIC is a form -- it's what happens to your blood, particularly if a child or a baby has a really severe infection, a lot of your clotting factors or the bits in your blood that help the
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: blood to clot don't work properly or just disappear and that constellation, that group of things, is called DIC.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So my plan: I've crash-called [Dr B], so that means I've called or I have asked somebody to call my consultant urgently because I appreciate the potential seriousness of the situation. I've contacted haem --
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "haem" is haematology, so the doctors in the doctors, and technicians that look after blood products. I have contacted them to order FFP and platelets. So FFP and platelets are products that you can give to a child or a baby if there is a clotting disorder. So if this was the case that [Baby B] had an overwhelming infection where parts of her blood weren't working properly, I might need to give her extra ones quickly. Because I didn't know at that time, I have just asked them to make sure they've got them ready.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And I've written "awaiting coagulation". So that's me waiting the blood test, the coag test, to see if I need to give those two blood products.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have said, "Need BC". BC is blood culture, so we need to take a sample of her blood urgently to send to the lab to see if we can grow any bacteria or -- is there any signs of infection on that.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I have also planned to do a head ultrasound. So this would be for the following day or the next few days. This is if there is an overwhelming infection in the baby or the baby's had a tremendous collapse that's needing a lot of help, it can have consequences on the brain and sometimes you can see these by doing an ultrasound scan of the brain. You can do that through the baby's soft spot.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I've also asked for the parents to be called urgently. Personally, I tend to involve parents quite early on if the children (sic) is very unwell or particularly if it's unexpected. I had a low threshold to contact parents to ask them to come in.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Then the last one is "IV teicoplanin". Teicoplanin is an antibiotic -- sorry, teicoplanin and cefotaxime.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So those are two antibiotics that cover lots of different types of bacteria. She has got a long line in situ. A long line is like a straw, plastic straw that goes into the skin and then burrows internally and the tip of it is near the heart. It's a way of getting fluids, antibiotics, anything into the baby that needs it for a long period of time. So if you have cannula or piece of plastic in the skin, it doesn't last that long, whereas
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: a long line lasts longer. You can also put chemicals through it which are a little more irritant that you wouldn't be able to put through a shorter one and [Baby B] had a long line in already.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Does that suggest they were going to be administered via the long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have asked them to be, yes. So that's me saying we don't need to worry about getting any more access, we have access, so we can give the antibiotics that way.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Okay. Then we have another heading, "Bloods".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: These are the blood results that have come through. So the first set are the kidney function. "U&C" is urea and creatine. I have highlighted those because they're a little bit high but then we have had to do resuscitation on her so it is not hugely unexpected for them to be marginally high.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I'm going to pause you. When you say they're high, are they the ones on the left (overspeaking) the double line under them?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- abnormal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So they are the two that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That are abnormal --
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: -- stood out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Underneath I have written "CRP". That's the C-reactive protein. That is a protein marker that looks for inflammation. 1 is normal. So anything under 10 you don't tend to worry about. So at that time that tells me that there was no background of infection at that time.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: So even though that's on your list of possibilities, that's the result from the bloods that you took?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that time, yes. You would need to repeat it. So it doesn't say that there wasn't an infection, it just says at that moment in time when I took those bloods there wasn't overwhelming inflammation.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you, carry on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next set is PT, APTT and FIB. That's all the blood clotting results for coagulation I was referring to.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And they're -- I can't recall the normal numbers off the top of my head but I haven't underlined them so that tells me they would have been normal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next set is haemoglobin, so that is the full blood count. Haemoglobin, which is the red cells. The white count is the white cells. So they're all normal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Platelets. They're part of your clotting system.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: They're a little bit low and I've written underneath "clump". Quite often on the blood results the people that analyse it will say if they have seen them, I can't recall because I haven't got the result in front of me, but the fact I've written clump -- I assume that means on the result they said they had clumped and it's not unusual it's just, unfortunately, the test doesn't always work.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: D-dimer is "awaiting" -- that's another part of the clotting I'm waiting to come back. And then the repeat gas that I've done is normal.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You told us that [Baby B] recovered very quickly from this episode. Did you continue to monitor through the shift, through the remainder of the night shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have. Without seeing my notes, I can't recall if I've documented anything, but from personal experience if I've had to be involved that much with a child, then I would have stayed fairly close by unless I was called away.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And had you had contact with [Baby B] before this episode took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall without looking at my notes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: All right. I have no more questions, but if you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Lambie, you were involved in the responses to both [Baby A]'s and [Baby B]'s collapses on successive nights; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Just a few questions about [Baby A] and a few questions about [Baby B]. Dealing with the first night, 8 June, you arrived, didn't you, as Dr Harkness and nursing staff were already providing respiratory support?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And to be clear about this, you were there, however, before Dr Jayaram attended?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And Dr Jayaram is the senior consultant, as it happens, who was crash-called to come to this event?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: You remained there as resuscitation was conducted with [Baby A], didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And you took part in that resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And you were there until the point when collectively the decision was taken that it had to stop?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And after that, your involvement ceased?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: All right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The following night, into the early hours, in fact, of the morning of the 10th, you were involved in responding to what happened with [Baby B], weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I'm interested to ask you what it was in particular that you noticed about [Baby B], the discolouration.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I recall that she was a very -- what we call, dusky, so a grey-white, colour, and then there were patches of discolouration of the skin that were sort of reddy/purple. It would flash up, it last around 10 seconds, disappear and then reappear, and it was flitting round her body.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: I'm assisted by your statement that you have had the chance of reading before you came into court, but that was something which stood out with [Baby B], wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And you describe it as "a very strange and profound colour change"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And it was something that you hadn't ever seen before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And something you haven't seen since or you hadn't seen since is at the time you made your witness statement?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have seen similar rashes but not like that, no.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And the description you gave, and let me just check we're clear with this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It was very grey and pale looking, flushes of what looked like bruising or reddening under the skin."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And they would appear for maybe 10 seconds and then go but appear somewhere else?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Is that right? And it struck you really because you hadn't seen anything like that before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: This is just for you to explain to us -- I'm not challenging anything you say about your notes -- but if a doctor sees something like that, would you expect them to make a note of it in their record of what took place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's a very difficult question to answer. If it had an outcome then yes. It does depend on the situation at hand, what you document.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: All right. Shall we have a look at what you documented just with regard to that, please? We'll look, please, if we could at S221. We've just looked at it in fact.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we go to the first page, please. We just come down to see what you put, Dr Lambie. Scroll down the page. We can see you've put in fact:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Had acute apnoea..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that "with no warning"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: "Widespread purple discolouration of skin with white patches."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And that's the reference to the rash that you saw?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Plainly, something that you considered significant enough to put into these notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Because it was something that was a remarkable feature, first of all, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And you would expect that to be put in if a remarkable feature like that is identified?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's something that I wouldn't be surprised to see, yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And in fact, you made reference later on when you were talking about intubation, the importance of putting it in as a record so that people who come afterwards can see what has happened?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: And the notes are important for that as well, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Should they include, so far as you're able, relevant observations as to what you have seen (overspeaking) took place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Good practice would be.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: Good practice would be, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: In fact the discolourations that you saw began to fade within 10 minutes/20 minutes, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, within -- each one was there for about 10 seconds and would disappear.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: But overall, was there a period when her colouration began to settle back to something like normal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, so her background, the greyness, the whiteness overall, about 30 minutes later.
blocks.speaker: LAMBIE

blocks.text: About 30 minutes. And if we just scroll down, please, what we have in the notes, can we see in the centre of the page:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Gradual improvement in perfusion over the next 30 minutes"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram, your present status, please?

blocks.text: I qualified in June 1990.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And how long have you been at Chester in your capacity as a consultant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I started as a consultant at the Countess of Chester in December 2004.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, in April 2009 I took on the role of what at the time was called clinical director and then got re-branded as lead clinician, which essentially means administrative head of department.

blocks.text: That's the department of paediatrics.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you have responsibilities in addition to paediatrics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As well as my clinical work as clinical director/lead clinician I was very much involved in management, so development of the service, dealing with incidents, liaising with senior management if we had issues around staffing or equipment or general service development I was the point of contact with more senior management and if they had issues that any needed to feed back to us I was the point of contact for them. blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I want to ask you to cast your mind back, please, to June of 2015. How many consultants would there have been in the department then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that time we had seven consultant paediatricians working in the acute paediatric service.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. You're the first consultant from whom we've heard. We have heard something of how the doctors worked and the nurses worked. What was the shift rota for consultants?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So as consultants, the way we worked is that for -- at that time, one week in every seven we were called paediatrician of the week or people would refer to it as the hot work. In that hot week, which at that time we started on a Monday morning and carried on through to the following Monday morning, we would be responsible for acute admissions. So we were responsible for the care of children on the children's assessment unit, who'd been referred by A&E and by GPs. We were responsible for the care of children on the children's ward. We were responsible for the babies on the neonatal unit as well and babies on the post-natal wards.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The way it worked was that during the day, Monday to Friday, in theory we had our normal fixed commitments cancelled, so we wouldn't have had outpatient clinics.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In theory we wouldn't have had scheduled meetings, which meant that we were free to deal with things as they came.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The way it worked during the hot week is that Monday 8.30 to 4.30 or 8.30 to 4 we would be responsible for everything: overseeing everything, overseeing the work of the junior doctors. We'd have a handover at 4 o'clock and there would be another consultant who would be on call from 4 o'clock to the following morning. So that person could be called at any time if they were needed.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Then on weekends we did, as paediatrician of the week, a weekend on call where we started taking the on-call from Friday morning and we finished being on call on the Monday morning.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, that meant that in theory we could potentially be in hospital the whole time, but usually it meant that you were there during the days, but not at nights, but you could get called in at any time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The rest of the cycle in the 6 weeks we did our day-to-day jobs. So we had our outpatient clinics, we were teaching medical students, teaching and training, audit meetings, management meetings, quality and governance meetings, the general day-to-
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: day admin. And when you weren't on your hot week, we did what was called a 1:7 rota, so out of hours one of us, 1 in 7 on average, would be on call out of hours.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When you were on call out of hours were you expected to be within a certain distance of the hospital?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The contract states that you have to be either within 10 miles -- I think it's 10 miles of the hospital or be available within 30 minutes if you're called in in an emergency. Most of us were well within those two.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Consultants who lived further away actually lived on site in one of the flats in the hospital when they were on call --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- so we were easily accessible.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right. I want to deal please with 8 June specifically and a child called [Baby A]. Do you remember what your position, your role, your rota was that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So on that day I was down to be the consultant on call.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The way we worked at that time on Mondays is that the -- and I can't remember whether I had taken over as paediatrician of the week because I don't think I did because I was on call that Monday. What would happen is that on the Monday, the person who had been paediatrician of the week would finish at lunchtime.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: They'd have handed over to another paediatrician of the week. I think on that day, because I was on call, I actually took over covering for emergencies in the afternoon. I was actually in an outpatient clinic, which is -- it's a small unit, it's next door to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall receiving an emergency alert in respect of [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That was later on in the evening. I'd had a couple of discussions about X-rays regarding [Baby A] through the afternoon. I had an emergency, I think it was some time after 8 pm. I can't remember the exact time. It's stated in my statement.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm conscious that you will have discussed his treatment both before and when you arrived, but I'm going to concentrate, if I can, on just what you saw and what you heard in the course of that evening. Okay?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you want it from the time I got the emergency call?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I can probably help with you that because if we can go to the sequence of events, please, and tile number 202.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you can see there, the swipe data suggests that you entered the neonatal unit at 8.34 that evening.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can you tell us, please, why you attended?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I'd had an emergency call from the neonatal unit to attend. Dr David Harkness was one of my registrars, who was in attendance with [Baby A] -- sorry, am I allowed to refer to the babies by name?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's easier and I think it's the right thing to do.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I was asked to attend by David Harkness. I can't remember exactly who called me. I suspect that the call had gone to switchboard and they'd paged me with a voice message through my pager or phone to come direct to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When I arrived, Dr Harkness was there. I think by that stage he had intubated. He'd told me that what had happened was that whilst he was attending to another baby and he was scrubbed, which meant that he was in sterile gear doing a procedure, he had been called because [Baby A] had become apnoeic. [Baby A] was on what was called CPAP, which is non-invasive ventilation to support his breathing, but this had happened very suddenly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: He had become apnoeic, Dr Harkness had stopped what he was doing and had attended. I believe that [Baby A] had had resuscitation, some breaths given through a Neopuff, which is a non-invasive mask, to give some breaths, and the chest had moved. And because he wasn't breathing spontaneously Dr Harkness had intubated him.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So I think at the time I arrived, and correct me if I'm wrong, he had been intubated. Dr Harkness told me that he'd actually seen the tube pass through the vocal cords, which is important, because sometimes endotracheal tubes can be misplaced, but if you actually visualise it going through the vocal cords, then you know it's in the right place. [Baby A] was receiving breaths through that tube with the Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I noted that [Baby A] looked very pale. I noted that the chest was moving and moving equally and I noted at that time he did have a heart rate on the monitor of 90 to 100 and the electrical
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: rhythm noted on the monitor was what we call sinus rhythm, which is a normal electrical rhythm. That's the normal electrical activity of the heart.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can I just ask you to pause there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Apnoeic, can you just explain to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Apnoeic means that basically you've stopped breathing, so there was no evidence of any spontaneous breathing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the heart rate that you'd have expected?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We normally expect a heart rate in a baby to be above 100. Now, the heart rate can be lower and it can be normal. It's important that the heart rate is enough to be able to pump blood around the body. In this situation the baby was apnoeic and so breaths had been given. And the heart rate was 90 to 100, which is a little bit lower than one would expect, but it was lower than it had been before he became apnoeic. So it had dropped slightly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And then you started to tell us about electrical activity.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So obviously, the way the heart muscle works is a very coordinated pulse of electrical impulses that go through to the different chambers of the chart. When we look at an ECG trace, we know from the patterns on the ECG whether that electrical conduction is moving as it should be, the various waves we call the P waves, the QRS complex and the T wave. And on the monitor at that time, although the heart rate was lower than one would expect, the pattern of the electrical activity was normal electrical activity.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You can sometimes get abnormalities of electrical conduction that can lead to the heart not beating properly and they can be associated with fairly typical and well-recognised abnormal patterns on the ECG trace.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So remind us, please, how did you interpret what you could -- could you see this on a monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, you could see this on a monitor above the incubator and the rhythm was -- you could see a P wave followed by QRS complexes, followed by a T wave. So this, at the point I arrived, is what we called sinus rhythm, which is the normal electrical activity. That doesn't necessarily mean that the
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: heart is beating effectively; you can see electrical activity and the heart muscle may not be pumping properly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm just going to ask you to pause again. I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A note is being made elsewhere of what you're saying and I think they're just -- my fault entirely -- they are just struggling to keep up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, I'll try and slow down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It is my fault, please don't apologise. You were telling us about the heart muscle.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you could pick up there, a little bit more slowly, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the reason the pumping chambers of the heart pump is because of coordinated electrical impulses that start in the atria, which are the two chambers at the top of the heart, that pump blood into the big chambers, the ventricles. There's a pacemaker, called the sinus, that sends an impulse to a thing called the node, which then sends an impulse through the rest of the heart. We know from the ECG, which is the heart tracing, the curves and lines that you see on the strips, whether that sequence of electricity is functioning as it should. We call normal electrical activity sinus rhythm. And in sinus rhythm you see a P wave, followed by a QRS complex, followed by a T wave. That's the classical picture.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When I looked at the monitor, when I arrived --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Bit more slowly again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just slow it down a bit, (a), because it's complex to listen to, but it's even more difficult to transcribe it and there is live transcription going on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Absolutely, not a problem.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When I looked at the monitor, what I could see, although the heart rate was lower than I would expect, was what we call sinus rhythm. So it was clear that there was a P wave, followed by a QRS complex, followed by a T wave. Which suggests that there wasn't -- whatever was causing the lower heart rate, it wasn't a problem with electrical conduction through the heart.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You can have evidence of electrical conduction without the heart actually pumping, but most of the time when we see something on
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: a monitor, if you can hear heart sounds and feel pulses, in that situation, the heart muscle will be working. There is a situation known as pulseless electrical activity where you see electrical activity, but actually the heart muscle isn't pumping, which can occur.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: There wasn't anything, when I came, to suggest abnormal electrical activity. You can get problems with the pumping of the heart muscle related to abnormal electrical activity as well, but when you see those, you will see fairly stereotypical patterns on the ECG that you know are associated with some of those abnormal electrical patterns.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. So what you could see was normal?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I think you described -- [Baby A] was pale?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was pale, he was pale. And what I didn't really give any clinical significance to at the time was sort of unusual patches of discolouration. It's interesting because it's the first time I'd seen that and I didn't actually think at the time it was of any clinical significance, so didn't actually record it in the notes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But they were definitely there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I can't remember how long those were present for throughout the process of resuscitation. But what I did notice was that, as well as being pale, he was quite floppy as well. There was no obvious spontaneous movement. And he definitely didn't seem to have been trying to breathe spontaneously.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When we intubate babies, as you can imagine, it's not a particularly pleasant sensation, we've got a tube between the vocal cords, so for a baby to tolerate intubation suggests that they are not really aware that it's happening, if that makes sense. When I very first started in paediatrics in the early 1990s, we routinely, when we intubated babies, didn't give any sedation, and I remember fully intubating babies who were fully conscious and them fighting and it was not a very nice experience. We don't do that anymore.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But in a resuscitation situation, if we're intubating a baby and the baby actually tolerates intubation, it's a sign that they probably haven't really felt you doing that. It's a sign that, in terms of their conscious level, it's lower than it might have been otherwise.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. So just going back to the unusual appearance, could you describe it in a bit more detail?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So obviously, when the circulation is poor or babies haven't got enough oxygen in their system, they will become -- they'll go from pink to pale to blue -- or the technical term is cyanosed. [Baby A] was very pale to blue, but there were unusual -- the best way to describe them is pink patches that appeared mainly, I recall, on the torso, on the abdomen, which seemed to sort of appear and disappear and flit around. And I'd never really seen anything like this before. But my focus at the time really was very much on what we call ABC: airway, breathing, circulation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So that's probably my best description of that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Are you able to say how long that went on for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't, I can't remember how long that went on for.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So you told us he was intubated. Tell us then, please, how his treatment progressed from there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What happened next was unusual in my experience and the reason I say it's unusual, and I'm going to -- I feel as if I'm giving the jury a medical school lecture, so I do apologise. But I'm going to take a step back to give some context to what I'm about to say.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Unlike in adults where the primary, most common cause of arrest is primarily a problem with the heart, babies and children can, but very rarely, have a primary heart problem, so -- I hope this doesn't happen -- I could collapse now and it would be unexpected.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Generally, when babies get as far as having apnoeas, arresting, it's usually the end point of other pathological processes. Usually, when a baby gets to that point, there have been signs leading up to the event that will have given us clues. So in a situation of, for example, dehydration or fluid depletion or blood loss, we will see the heart rate gradually go up over a period of time and that's the body's response to not having enough volume in the circulation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The heart is trying to maintain what is called the cardiac output. The cardiac output is a function of how fast your heart is beating and how much blood is being pumped out with each contraction. And if, to give the example of dehydration, your cardiac output is lower because there's less being pumped out, your body will speed your heart rate up.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What was unusual in this situation was that the heart rate had been fairly stable and this happened suddenly. Sometimes, particularly in a situation where there may be infection around, you can get blood vessels that become leaky peripherally, blood vessels that dilate up and your blood pressure drops. But again in this situation, there hadn't to this point been any observations that [Baby A] had had cooler hands and feet, there hadn't been any situation to suggest that he'd become faster with his breathing, slower with his breathing. His observations had been stable up to the --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Some water?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I thought that's what you were gesturing. Don't apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Sorry about that.
blocks.speaker: JUROR

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you but it had to be done.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So this situation was unusual because it seemed that in the sequence of events the first thing that had happened was that [Baby A] had become apnoeic, he'd stopped breathing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So if babies who are premature become apnoeic there's a number of things that we have to consider could cause that. We know that premature babies can sometimes forget to breathe. The respiratory centre that makes us breathe without thinking about it isn't mature and they can have what are known as apnoeas of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Generally, if you have an apnoea of prematurity, it usually stimulates the baby and they'll start breathing again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Sometimes --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Stimulate, what does that mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You prod them, for want of a better description. So you do something. If that doesn't work then, if it's an apnoea of prematurity, giving them some breaths again, if the apnoea is picked up and their oxygen levels have already begun to drop, giving them some breaths, getting gas into their lungs, they will start to breathe again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This was unusual because he had not really been reported to be having any apnoeic spells but he had the apnoea.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The next thing then is if you become apnoeic and you're not breathing effectively, then ultimately you are not going to get
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: oxygen into your lungs, carbon dioxide out. If you don't get oxygen into your lungs the blood that is pumping through your lungs won't be able to pick up that oxygen, therefore the blood going around your body doesn't have as much oxygen, and therefore you can spiral downwards.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So usually in a situation, if a baby's had a prolonged apnoea, which is an apnoea of prematurity, when you bag them, so a colloquial term, when you use the Neopuff and breathe for them and you are basically inflating the lungs and getting gas into the lungs and you've got a heart that is pumping enough to pump blood through the lungs, what should happen is that the blood travelling through the lungs should become oxygenated, should go back round the body, and you should turn the problem around.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What was unusual here is that in spite of absolutely appropriate and timely manoeuvres from the team who were there at the time he had an apnoea, and they documented that the chest was moving, so gas must have been going in and out of the lungs, the heart rate, instead of picking up, continued to drop.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You can sometimes have acute events and certainly in a baby on CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure, a non-invasive ventilation where we are blowing a pressure to help to keep the lungs open, there is a risk of what's called a pneumothorax, which is essentially where one of the small pockets at the end of the lungs, the alveoli, can pop. So air goes into the lung and leaks out of the lung and accumulates in the space between the lung and the chest wall. And in that situation babies can become apnoeic, but again you would usually notice -- the first sign of that wouldn't be that they suddenly became apnoeic, you'd see a sudden increase in the amount of oxygen that they were needing to maintain their oxygen saturations. And if that's not picked up then it might lead to respiratory arrest and cardio-respiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Again, this didn't really fit with pneumothorax, (1) because it was sudden and (2), the comment was made that both sides of the chest were moving when the lungs were being inflated with the Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you've got a pneumothorax, you don't really see that side of the chest moving, you'll see reduced movement on one side and reduced breath sounds on one side.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So this was unusual to me because this didn't really fit with anything I'd ever seen in a newborn or a premature baby before. I have seen lots of babies have apnoeas, I have seen lots of babies who need to have Neopuff ventilations. I have seen some babies who don't respond, and if they don't respond, it's usually because there's been something else going on in terms of
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: pneumothoraces or evolving RDS, the lung condition that premature babies get through maturity.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But as I said at the start of this bit of the lecture, this didn't fit because it was very, very sudden. It didn't fit. All these other things you would usually see as the end point of other things that had been going on prior to this and you would have had clues from observations that had been made.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And even when [Baby A] was intubated, so we knew that gas was going in and out of the lungs, what should have happened is his heart rate should have picked up. And what actually happened was his heart rate began to drop.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we generally say if the heart rate drops below 60, even if the heart is pumping, it is probably not going to be pumping effectively to get blood both up to the lungs and around the body, and then we start cardiac compressions.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It still doesn't fit, to me, with any disease process that I've ever seen, learned about, read about, in my career, why he didn't respond as he should have done.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: One of the things, and I'll take another step -- and this comes more perhaps from resuscitation of older children. We have a sort of an algorithm to think through in terms of the sorts of things that could cause these unusual collapses. We talk about the four Hs and the four Ts.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So we talk about hypoxia. Hypoxia is when enough oxygen in your system and hypoxia can lead to collapse, but actually, until the point he became apnoeic, his oxygen saturations were okay. So although hypoxia was a subsequent thing, it doesn't really fit as a cause of the collapse.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Hypovolaemia. So if you have not had enough fluid and your circulation is empty, that can lead to things, but in that situation you would begin to see, well before it led to any acute consequence, signs that hypovolaemia was happening in terms of feeling cold peripherally, an increase in heart rate over time as well, and it would be unusual for that to present with an acute apnoeic episode out of the blue.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Electrolyte imbalances, so hypokalaemia, (inaudible: coughing), so abnormal potassium levels, abnormal calcium levels. Again, there was no evidence of any issues around electrolyte problems.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And hypothermia. Hypothermia is really on the list.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is more sort of older children that are found lying in the park in the middle of winter unconscious and we know that
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: hypothermia can sometimes cause arrest and it's usually because of cardiac arrhythmias where we don't see sinus rhythm and there was no evidence of that --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can I ask you to pause. It's very intensive and there's a lot of information. So is my impression right that you go through, and we're going to go through a few more in a minute, when you are faced with a situation you look at the alternatives and whether you can eliminate them or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think the important thing, first of all, is to deal with the acute problem. We secure the airway, breathing, circulation. You have to make sure that you can get all of that right first before then thinking, I wonder what's caused all of this. You could argue surely we need to work out what's going on first before we can do something about it. But in these acute situations it's very much: get the airway/breathing/circulation right and then think about why has this happened. Because if you try to be too clever and stand there for 10 minutes thinking, I wonder what's causing it, by the time you have worked it out, it might be too late. And the basic interventions at the start of all of these things are the same regardless.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So we are thinking through things and I mentioned the four Hs and we also think about the four Ts. So tension pneumothorax. That's where one of the alveoli/lung sacs pops and the lung collapses down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: There's no evidence of that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Toxicity. So could this be due to some kind of overdose of a drug or anything else that's gone in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's always something you have to consider. It's unusual on a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: A very rare situation, which I've never seen in a newborn, called cardiac tamponade, where essentially a leak develops in the wall of the heart muscle and blood leaks out into the sac around the heart so the heart can't beat. Again, I have never seen that in neonatology.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The last T is what is known as thromboembolic phenomenon. That is classically if you have a clot in your leg and it flies off — the mechanism there is that would then get into the right side of the heart, get into the blood circulation to the lungs, and prevent blood from flowing into the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, again, I have never seen that happen in newborns in my life because generally it's something when you have been on a longhaul flight and you have a clot. So it didn't really fit at the
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: time with any of these things. But that wasn't really the foremost of my thoughts at that time. The foremost of my thoughts was to deal with what we were seeing in front of us.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And at the point the heart rate dropped down to 60 we switch into -- we have fairly clear algorithms of what we do and when and we went into that mode. So CPR went on, CPR meaning breaths in conjunction with cardiac compressions. And the idea of that is you are basically doing the heart's job for it. You are trying, in simple terms, to keep blood flowing and to keep the baby breathing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But in spite of those efforts, and in spite of various drugs that were given -- adrenaline, sodium bicarbonate, glucose -- we give what's called volume as well. So as we're thinking through those Hs and Ts, we give what is called a bolus of normal saline. If the circulation is empty, you pour more into the circulation and that should help things to pick up. If the sugar's low, we give glucose. If you have very high acid levels in the blood from having prolonged periods of low oxygen and anaerobic respiration, we will give sodium bicarbonate because if there's a very acidic environment it can affect how the heart muscle functions.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But in spite of all of these interventions, he didn't turn around.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Pausing there, I'm sorry, you mentioned I think adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So what -- just while we're on the point of what you can give and the effect, what would adrenaline do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Adrenaline is interesting and the use of adrenaline certainly in newborn resuscitation, when babies are first born, is controversial because everything's extrapolated from studies in adults and children. But essentially what adrenaline can do is stimulate the heart muscle. It might improve blood flow through the coronary arteries which carry blood to the heart. It basically helps to stimulate the heart.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In practice, in resuscitation in newborns, by the time we get to the stage where we are needing to use adrenaline in arrest situations, it's not very often that we have a successful outcome.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm sorry, when I interrupted you about adrenaline you were about to tell us the next stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So we gave adrenaline, I forget, it's in the statement, three or four rounds of it, I can't remember entirely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We would give glucose. There was no evidence of a low glucose. And again hypoglycaemia, a low glucose, would very rarely -- in fact I have never known it present with an acute apnoea.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Low blood sugars can sometimes cause a seizure, a fit. Seizures can present as apnoeas, but usually if a baby is having a seizure you would see the heart rate go up. So in a situation of a fit where you have abnormal electrical activity of the brain, you would see the heart rate go higher. So it didn't really fit with that.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: As I mentioned, sodium bicarbonate. I think really I can't think of a baby that I've looked after where we've got as far as using sodium bicarbonate in resuscitation where the outcome has been good in terms of actually getting the baby back or of long-term neurodevelopmental outcome.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So it was unusual because, for me, thinking back to what happened with [Baby A], it didn't fit with the usual patterns of what I would expect to happen.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I can't explain why he had the apnoea. It could have been just an apnoea of prematurity. But if it was, he should have responded, he probably wouldn't have even needed to have any artificial breaths given and then certainly when he had artificial breaths given and his chest was clearly moving, he should have picked up and he didn't. And then when his heart rate dropped, which still makes no sense to me, there should have been some response to some of the interventions that we did. It may not have been that we would have had a successful outcome, but I would anticipate with adrenaline, if the heart rate is still present, you would still see some response.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And later in the resuscitation we did see evidence of a heart rate and hear a heartbeat but it was ineffective, so we would still call that an arrest situation and it was short-lived.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It was a difficult situation because I'd not had any dealings with [Baby A] to that point. It was the first time that I'd really had any contact with his family, which is an awful situation to be in, in that situation as a paediatrician, when the first thing you have to say to a family is that, number 1, I'm not sure what's going on and, number 2, I don't think we're going to be able to bring him back.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you have that conversation with the family?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you discuss it amongst the other professionals?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely. In these situations, and thankfully they don't happen too often, it's very much a -- well, it should be a collaborative decision. It's certainly not for me as a consultant to say, I think we should stop and I don't care what anyone else thinks.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Ultimately, it's a decision between myself, my team and the family, and it's my job as a consultant to be as balanced and realistic as we possibly can. It's probably one of the worst parts of the job that I have to do as a consultant.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we know that you reached that point where you had that conversation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely. Generally, after about 20 minutes, we know that actually we could potentially carry on and there have been situations I've been in where we have carried on and children have got a heart rate back and they've survived, but generally with a lot of neurodevelopmental problems. And occasionally you'll get a child who is a miracle baby and does really well, but in this situation we never really got much back and I think we went on -- again, it's in my statement, but I think we attempted resuscitation for well over 30 minutes in this situation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When efforts were abandoned or -- what's the practice then? What do the clinicians do at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what we generally do is at that point, having discussed things with the family, is talk to the family, explain things and really give them some private time with the baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can I just -- sorry, I've just remembered one other thing that we did during resuscitation. I was talking about thinking about why these things happen. One of the things that we did -- two things that we did during the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I think people may already have talked about the umbilical venous catheter, which we put in through the umbilicus to give fluids and medications. It had gone into one of the veins towards the liver and it was slightly longer than it should be. So we just pulled it back slightly. It's fine to give glucose through there but we don't want adrenaline going into the liver. So we pulled that back at the time there was no other source of emergency drug administration. And we also suggested taking the long line out -- and the reason for that is at this time we didn't know why this had happened and although I'd seen sinus
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: rhythm, so there was no evidence of an abnormal electrical rhythm, one of the complications that can happen with a long line, if it goes all the way into the right atrium, the chamber of the heart, is -- I mentioned this thing called the sinus, which is the pacemaker -- it can sit on the sinus and cause abnormal rhythms. And given we didn't know what was going on and at that point the long line was unnecessary, I said, well, let's take the long line out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In retrospect, I actually don't think it was related to the long line at all in terms of the fact that there was never any abnormal electrical rhythm seen, but we did that as well. I should have mentioned that earlier.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That leads me on to equipment really because you told us you took the long line out. What's the best practice with equipment that the baby is already attached to the baby (overspeaking) UVC? So after death, is there a practice --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ordinarily we would, particularly in this situation, because it was unexplained and I knew that we would be -- I was going to discuss [Baby A] with the coroner, we would leave as much in as possible. So we should be leaving tubes and lines and things in as a matter of course. I can't remember what we did with [Baby A] but the long line came out in the course of resuscitation as an active decision.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It was left in we know.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right. So having withdrawn and left the family to be with the baby, any further involvement with either of the children?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, so after that, I spoke with Dr Harkness, my registrar, who was devastated because obviously he had done this procedure shortly before and he was really concerned that this had happened as a consequence of the long line he'd put in. We looked at the X-ray together and it was slightly longer in than one would want it to be, but certainly not in a position where it would have caused any abnormal heart rhythm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Pause there: which X-ray are we talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it must have been the X-ray that was done after the long line was put in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So when you say the long line --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- looking at the long line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just to look at the long line. I said to him I think it's extremely unlikely because (1) it's not in a position where you would expect it to cause a rhythm problem and (2) we didn't see any abnormal electrical activity.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Would you have expected to see that on the monitor when (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely. If the long line had caused a problem, (1) I wouldn't have expected an apnoea to be the first presentation, I would have expected to see an abnormal electrical rhythm first -- and usually if that's recognised your first intervention is to withdraw the long line a little bit so that is not in a position where it could be causing rhythm -and I have seen this many times, putting umbilical venous catheters in, where if they go in too far into the heart, you can actually see a change in rhythm and you pull it back and, you know, the rhythm becomes normal and there was no evidence of that at all.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So after that I then spoke to the coroner and I documented a number of thoughts in the notes about things that could have happened: could this have been a pneumothorax, could there be any evidence of infection or sepsis? But I really didn't -couldn't explain the sequence of -- why this sequence of events had happened.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I didn't explain why it had happened in the first place and I couldn't explain why the physiological responses as expected to appropriate and timely interventions did not happen as they should have done and I spoke with Mr Rheinberg, the coroner, that evening who said it was going to go to the coroners.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Very good. Dr Jayaram, I have no more questions for you. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes. And you have given us a very fulsome explanation, setting out why, for example, it was no fault of anyone involved in this resuscitation, in the course of the resuscitation, that [Baby A] died. You have gone to some lengths to explain that, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.speaker: MYERS
